vignette:
The Road She Can't Leave Behind

Maya is twenty-five years old and drives a city transit bus through the downtown core, a job she took eight months ago when she came home from her second deployment. She chose it, she says, because she needed to keep moving. Sitting still has never felt safe to her - not anymore.

Maya enlisted at eighteen, drawn by a sense of purpose and a family tradition of service. Her first deployment passed without catastrophic incident, and she returned home proud, if quieter than before. Her second tour was different. During a convoy operation in her twenty-third year, the vehicle ahead of her was struck by an IED. She watched the explosion from the driver's seat - close enough to feel the percussion in her chest, close enough to see what was left afterward. She pulled two of her unit members from the wreckage. One survived. She performed CPR on the other for eleven minutes on the side of a desert road before a medic told her to stop. She has not stopped seeing that face.

When Maya returned stateside, people told her she seemed fine. She smiled when she was supposed to. She moved into a small apartment, got her CDL, and started her route. But fine is not a word that fits what lives inside her. Most mornings she wakes between three and four a.m., her heart hammering, her sheets soaked through. The dreams are not always the convoy - sometimes they are stranger, more fragmented - but the feeling is always the same: that she is responsible for something she could not stop, and that it is happening again right now.

Driving the bus is the one place where the structure holds her together. She knows the route. She knows every stop, every turn. But the job carries its own dangers for her. When a car backfires or a passenger drops something metal on the floor, Maya's hands tighten on the wheel until her knuckles pale. Her vision narrows. For a few seconds she is not on a city street - she is back on that road, the air tasting of smoke and burning rubber. She has pulled the bus to the curb twice in the past month, telling passengers there was a mechanical issue, because she needed sixty seconds to breathe before she could continue.

Outside of work, her world has grown very small. She stopped returning calls from her friends from her unit - the ones who were there. She tells herself it's because she doesn't want to burden them, but the truth is that hearing their voices pulls her back to the place she is trying to outrun. She avoids the news, avoids action films, avoids the military recruitment billboard three blocks into her route that she has memorized the exact timing of so she can look away. Her apartment has two deadbolts and a chain. She sleeps with the light on.

What troubles Maya most - what she mentions in a low voice, as though ashamed of it - is that she no longer recognizes herself. She used to be someone who laughed easily, who called her mother every Sunday, who had plans. Now she describes herself as hollowed out. She feels detached from the people around her, watching them through glass, unable to locate the warmth she once had. She wonders sometimes if she left the most important part of herself on that road, and whether it is possible to get it back.

She comes to sessions on her days off, still in her transit authority jacket, still carrying the particular alertness of someone who has learned that the world can change in an instant. She is not fragile - Maya is, in fact, one of the most resilient people one is likely to meet. But resilience has its costs, and hers have been quietly accumulating since the day she was told to stop.
